title: The History of Al-Bundukani (The Crossbowman)

full_text:
Caliph Harun al-Rashid frequently patrolled the outskirts of Baghdad disguised as 'Al-Bundukani'—the Crossbowman—wearing a simple green huntsman's coat and carrying a polished hazel crossbow with clay pellets.

One twilight near the orchards of the Tigris, he observed a corrupt tax magistrate and four armed bailiffs surrounding the cottage of an impoverished date farmer named Sa'id. The magistrate was seizing the farmer's young daughter as collateral for an unlawful assessment.

Harun al-Rashid notched a clay pellet into his crossbow, stepped out of the olive groves, and cried:
'Halt! Release that maiden in the name of the law!'

The arrogant magistrate sneered: 'Who art thou, ragged archer, to question the magistrate of Baghdad?'
Al-Bundukani raised his crossbow, released the catch, and the clay pellet struck the magistrate's turban with lightning precision, knocking the heavy silk hat into the dust! A second pellet shattered the bailiff's drawn sword at the hilt!

The terrified bailiffs, thinking they were attacked by a legion of forest marksmen, scattered into the brush.
The farmer and his daughter fell to their knees:
'Noble huntsman, thou hast saved our family, but tomorrow the magistrate will return with a company of guards and destroy our house!'

Al-Bundukani handed Sa'id an ivory token carved with a falcon's claw:
'Fear not. Tomorrow morning, take this token to the Golden Gate of the Palace. Ask for Al-Bundukani.'

The next dawn, Sa'id presented the ivory token at the palace. The guards escorted him with royal ceremony into the Great Hall of Justice.
Seated upon the imperial throne was the huntsman in imperial robes of state!
Beside the throne stood the corrupt magistrate, trembling in iron chains.

Harun al-Rashid smiled down at the farmer:
'Sa'id, the bow of Al-Bundukani has reached its mark.'
The Caliph dismissed the magistrate, returned all extorted property to the farmers of the district, and endowed Sa'id's family with a hereditary grant of land.
The tale of Al-Bundukani was sung throughout Mesopotamia as a testament that justice watches even when darkness hides the oppressor.
moral: A sovereign's secret vigilance ensures that justice reaches the humble, turning oppression into deliverance.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "The History of Al-Bundukani"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
